reading.body:
Model liability is being catalogued by what a model does rather than how it was built, and the ten categories run from hiring bias to deepfake wire fraud.

The list divides into two kinds of exposure. One is decisions about people: biased outputs in hiring, mortgage processing, tenant screening and healthcare, diagnostic tools that miss a critical condition, and professional advice that is inaccurate. The other is autonomous action: agents that execute bad transactions or corrupt data, trading loops that trigger market losses, process control systems that make improper adjustments, generated code that ships security flaws, and chatbots that issue unauthorised discounts or defamatory statements. Deepfake wire fraud sits between the two, because a synthesised executive is used to move money.

Where liability lands is the part that matters for AI. It attaches to the deployer and the developer rather than to the model as an artifact, and it reaches into domains that already had established causes of action, such as hiring, lending, healthcare, professional advice and vehicle operation. Only one entry, industrial control misconfiguration in plants and refineries, concerns physical plant at all. None of the ten concerns power supply or data centre operations, so this material does not speak to compute or grid constraints directly.

What it does not provide is scale. There are no loss amounts, claim counts, insurers, jurisdictions or dates attached to any category, and all ten entries carry an empty source field. The record is also marked as a draft. Read it as a map of where liability is expected to attach, not as evidence of how much has already been paid.
